extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of 19th-century literature; literary students and general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and critical standards for assessing Romantic-era poets and novelists (exemplified by Lord Byron and Sir Walter Scott), focusing on style, morality, dramatic power, originality, tone, and relation to nature and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political bias / servility to power
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial partisanship that uses literature to back established authority (Legitimacy) and to 'put down the Spirit of the Age' rather than to serve humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing that functions as an apologetic for power or as a tool to suppress reform; literature should not 'administer charms and philtres to our love of Legitimacy' or intentionally promote fear of reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mottos and intertextual modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'good-nature of the mottos' — remembering and quoting many living authors (illustrious or obscure) but oneself — as an indirect sign of source and humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mottos and quotations in a way that acknowledges influences and places the work in literary context rather than as self-exaltation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose correctness and careful editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'innumerable and incessant instances of bad and slovenly English' in printed works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should read manuscripts, oversee the press, and retouch copy; slovenliness in language betrays negligence and weakens authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to nature and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for a writer 'who bows to the authority of nature, who appeals to actual objects, to moulder-ing superstitions, to history, observation, and tradition' rather than one who merely projects his own breast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground imagination in observation, history, and real objects; favour authors who let the world inform their art rather than making the world merely a foil for personal temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and range of sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a writer who 'takes in (or is willing to take in) the range of half the universe in feeling, character, description' instead of one who 'shuts himself up' in a single temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that portray varied people, situations, and emotions rather than those confined to the author's singular, recurrent moods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic power and scene-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic quality: Sir Walter Scott is called 'the most dramatic writer now living' while Byron is 'the least so.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic writing should present scenes, characters, and action that carry the reader into the world of the work; avoid pedantry and excessive authorial intrusions that prevent dramatic immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / transparency of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between Sir Walter's 'perfectly transparent' style and Lord Byron's 'opaque' colouring: transparent prose lets the reader 'look through' to nature, whereas opaque splendour can obscure it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity that reveals subject and landscape; ornament should not prevent the reader from perceiving the object of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity and force vs sustained masterly whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Byron's distinguishing quality is 'Intensity' and 'force of style' but he 'seldom gets beyond' this and 'has not produced any regular work or masterly whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensity and force are virtues, but should be balanced with planning and unity so that works achieve coherence and enduring form rather than momentary stimulation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan, revision, and polished accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer ought to 'prepare any plan beforehand' and 'revise and retouch' to achieve 'polished accuracy' — the lack of which is criticized in Byron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with design and revise diligently; the absence of planning and retouching undermines the production of a 'masterly whole.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic characterization versus author-centric portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: Scott 'gives us man as he is' across 'almost every variety,' whereas Byron 'makes man after his own image' and produces 'everlasting centos of himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value character-drawing that shows a range of humanity rather than recurring figures who are merely permutations of the author's own temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral influence and emancipation of prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's moral worth: Scott is praised as 'one of the greatest teachers of morality ... by emancipating the mind from petty, narrow, and bigotted prejudices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the social and moral effect of literature — does it broaden sympathy, reduce prejudice, and instruct humanity toward improvement?

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined, pointed satire versus mere insolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Byron's satire (e.g. English Bards and Scotch Reviewers) is called 'dogmatical and insolent, but without refinement or point' — mere name-calling or degrading appeals to low means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be incisive and artful; avoid petulant abuse, coarse familiarity, or low insinuations unworthy of literary wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone management and avoidance of gratuitous desecration
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Byron's habit to 'hallow in order to desecrate' — raising expectation of genius or virtue only to 'dash them to the earth again' and make a 'pitiful hoax' of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain coherence of tone; do not purposefully elevate and then profanely undercut the reader's trust for mere effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject-matter to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'poetry moves best within the circle of nature and received opinion' and that 'speculative theory and subtle casuistry are forbidden ground' to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects congenial to poetic treatment (nature, received sentiments, human feeling); avoid forcing abstruse metaphysical casuistry into verse where it does not fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic essentials for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Byron's plays are criticized for lacking 'the essence of the drama' and for abounding 'in speeches and descriptions' that 'have neither action, character, nor interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should include action, distinct character, and interest that project beyond the poet's own mind; mere rhetorical speeches do not constitute drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between ornament and substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Juan's effect is 'owing to the force of the serious writing, and to the oddity of the contrast between that and the flashy passages' — jarring discontinuities between high and low elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that ornament, flashes of parody, or comic interlards serve the substance rather than producing disruptive contrasts that weaken overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge merit by intrinsic qualities, not external rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of 'the satire of a person of birth and quality, who measures all merit by external rank' and uses rank to degrade others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literary merit on intrinsic artistic and moral grounds rather than by the social rank or station of author or subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid courting shock and scandal for popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Byron is reproached for seeking to 'shock the public' and to 'force them to admire in spite of decency and common sense' — courting notoriety rather than true appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aim primarily to provoke or scandalize as a means to fame; writing should not sacrifice decency or substance for ephemeral applause.
